Physical Education | Years 12–13 | October 2026   Page 1

About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Physical Education Years 12–13 of
the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Physical Education Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Physical Education Years 12–13 is proposed
to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Physical Education Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12
from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Physical Education, students are taught the anatomical and biophysical                     Physical Education leads to pathways in sport sciences, sport coaching and
  science of movement, and how physical skills are produced, learned, adapted,                  leadership, health and physical activity promotion, community health, fitness, and
  and experienced across the lifespan. Physical Education examines how                          sport performance.
  leadership frameworks, coaching and sport pedagogy, and sport psychology
  shape inclusive, adaptive, and performance-focused physical activity experiences
  and events. Students are taught to analyse social and cultural influences on
  physical activity and apply theoretical, scientific, and practical knowledge of
  leadership, coaching, and the psychology of movement to design intentional and
  meaningful physical activity experiences and events.

Students are taught to integrate knowledge of how physical movement is produced
and adapted, through the study of anatomy, biomechanics, physiological factors, and
psychology. Students are taught how to develop performance, tactical and technical
skill, leadership, and coaching. They examine how norms and structures in sport and
physical activity have changed over time and place and how adaptive technologies
have enhanced participation.

Physical Education provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse
complex physical activity contexts and integrate concepts in practical, contextualised
ways. Students design, adapt, and evaluate coaching, leadership, and training
responses using reflective and evidence-informed reasoning.

As students progress through Years 12–13, they integrate disciplinary concepts,
experiences, observations, and data to analyse and evaluate performance, strategies,
and training principles in written form. This enables them to make justified judgements
and recommendations and communicate insight across personal, cultural,
community, and societal contexts.

 Disciplinary writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Physical Education, accurate application of concepts and terminology enables precise and purposeful written explanation and evaluation of performance, well-being, and training. Writing integrates
 evidence and reasoned analysis to form justified conclusions, while reflection, goal setting, and purposeful note-making operate as ongoing written practices that track progress, refine thinking, and
 support informed decisions to improve performance over time.

The teaching of all knowledge and practices is compulsory. However, schools can
determine how learning is organised across the year, including integrating content
from multiple elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth.
Examples within the teaching sequence in brackets signified with ‘e.g.’ are provided
as guidance only; as long as the intended knowledge and practices are met, schools
and teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local
environments, iwi and hapū connections, student interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to set out what subject-
specific literacy is to be taught. It is organised into a knowledge component that is
consistent across all year levels and a practice component sequenced across years.
